evaluation.positioning_hook: A sleep-deprived boarding-school student uncovers a dorm-room curse that erases forgotten kids from existence, then must choose whether to save his friend or vanish himself.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean horror engine with an immediate hook: a room that makes students disappear and a ticking clock tied to 1:11. The audience is narrower than a broad studio horror because the script leans more eerie and introspective than splashy, but the core fear is easy to sell.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early in the opening Room 111 sequence and stays legible: a dorm mystery, an eleven-year pattern, and a notebook that can transfer the curse. The rules are unusual but understandable, and the final reveal gives the premise a clean mythic shape.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ryan has a usable internal contradiction — he wants to matter but behaves like someone already half-erased — and James Walker is a strong antagonist presence. The supporting cast is functional, but the script is more built on mood and premise than on a deeply differentiated ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The boarding-school dorm setting, the 1:11 motif, and the idea of disappearance as social invisibility give the script a fresh angle inside familiar horror grammar. It is not radically unfamiliar, but the emotional metaphor is specific enough to feel authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The investigation into Zach, the yearbook pattern, and the Room 111 confrontation create a steady escalation with clear reveals. The middle section is more procedural than propulsive at times, but the mystery keeps paying off in new information.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The strongest idea is the curse feeding on students who have already started disappearing socially, which makes the supernatural threat feel psychologically inevitable. The notebook mechanic and the eleven-year cycle are memorable, even if the broader horror architecture is familiar.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The dorm, roll-call desk, curfew rules, yearbooks, and transfer records create a workable institutional world with enough texture to support the mystery. Still, the setting mostly functions as a container for the curse rather than a fully layered social ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct eerie, hushed register: fluorescent hallways, silence breaks, mirrored reflections, and Ryan’s voiceover about sleep deprivation and invisibility. It knows what kind of unease it wants and stays close to that frequency.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The curse is clearly a metaphor for depression, social erasure, and the fear of being unnoticed, and the script keeps folding those ideas back into the plot. The James Walker reveal adds a deeper layer without overexplaining the mythology.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ryan and Rhea give the script its emotional spine, and James provides a strong adversarial relationship, but most other characters are utility players. The story is not built as an ensemble engine; it lives primarily on Ryan’s isolation and one key connection.

lead_characters.name: Ryan
lead_characters.demographics: Teen male, high-school boarding student, likely 16-18.
lead_characters.hook: A sleep-deprived, emotionally detached boarding-school kid who moves through the dorm like he’s already half invisible. Ryan’s real conflict is not just solving the Room 111 mystery — it’s confronting how much of himself has already gone missing before the supernatural threat even reaches him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young lead in a contained genre breakout: internalized, reactive, then finally explosive in the Room 111 confrontation. It gives an actor the chance to play numbness, panic, guilt, and a late-breaking moral choice in one role.

lead_characters.name: Rhea
lead_characters.demographics: Teen female, high-school student, Ryan’s peer and emotional confidante.
lead_characters.hook: Rhea is the script’s human counterweight — observant, underplayed, and quietly carrying her own sense of disappearance. She’s not just the love interest or helper; she’s another kid who feels socially unheld, which makes her final note land as both plot turn and emotional wound.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a strong emotional aftertaste, similar to the best grounded teen-support turns in elevated horror. The showcase is restraint: she gets to play subtext, withheld confession, and the devastating reveal that she’s been fading too.

lead_characters.name: James Walker
lead_characters.demographics: Male, appears late-teen to early-30s but reveals a much older trapped identity.
lead_characters.hook: A trench-coated, unnervingly calm figure who functions like the room’s resident prophet and predator. James is compelling because he is both threat and warning: a kid who chose the wrong bargain and now speaks like someone who has spent years rationalizing it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a performance showcase in the vein of a charismatic horror antagonist who gets to monologue with precision and menace. The role offers the actor a rare blend of authority, bitterness, and tragic self-justification.

lead_characters.name: Mrs. Wesman
lead_characters.demographics: Adult female, dorm office staff member.
lead_characters.hook: The institutional face of the dorm — polite, procedural, and just vague enough to feel complicit without ever fully tipping into villainy. She gives the school its bureaucratic texture and becomes one of the script’s best sources of quiet dread because she normalizes the abnormal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong character-actor role in the tradition of the authority figure who seems harmless until the audience realizes how much she knows. The appeal is playing calm institutional control with a hairline crack of menace.

lead_characters.name: Mr. Brusco
lead_characters.demographics: Adult male, dorm staff / hall desk authority.
lead_characters.hook: A casual, almost jokey adult presence who helps sell the dorm as a place where kids are monitored but not truly seen. He’s useful because he makes the world feel lived-in while also reinforcing how easy it is for a disappearance to pass as routine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that lets an actor play everyday authority with an undercurrent of unease. It’s a compact, scene-stealing part if cast with someone who can make small behavior feel suspicious.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Henzy
lead_characters.hook: A warm, ordinary school presence who helps the script contrast normal attendance with supernatural erasure. She’s not written as a major player, but she matters because she embodies the system that keeps moving even when students vanish from it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean supporting role for an actor who can make routine school authority feel emotionally real. The showcase is subtlety: she has to feel like part of the machine without becoming faceless.

lead_characters.name: Jeff
lead_characters.demographics: Teen male, dorm student and peer.
lead_characters.hook: A comic-pressure release who also helps normalize the dorm’s social ecosystem. Jeff gives the script a little friction and levity, but he also reinforces the larger theme that everyone is only half-paying attention to everyone else.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a useful supporting role for an actor with timing and a naturalistic teen voice. The appeal is being the guy who can pivot from comic texture to eerie obliviousness.

casting_characteristics: adult authority figures in dorm/school roles

technical.vfx_details: Simple shadow appearances, light flicker effects, mirror/reflection beats, and a few transition-style visual moments; no heavy creature or environment work.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical lighting flicker, door movement, sound design for silence drops, breathing, phone-call distortion, and a few blood-smear details.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: contained genre title for streaming-first launch or specialty theatrical with horror audience upside.

budget.note: Mostly interiors, contemporary wardrobe, no stunt load, and only minor VFX for shadows, mirrors, and flicker effects. The main cost pressure is night photography and the need to make one dorm corridor feel ominous for extended stretches.

casting.note: Ryan has to carry the movie with a very specific mix of numbness, anxiety, and late-film conviction, while James needs real menace without turning into a generic horror villain. The teen ensemble also needs to feel age-true enough that the dorm world sells instantly.

development.note: The mythology is clear enough to follow, but the script depends on the audience accepting a metaphorical rule set: social invisibility becomes literal disappearance. The ending also asks for a clean emotional landing on Rhea’s note and the final Room 111 reset.

comp_set.title: The Black Phone
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the contained, youth-centered horror lane where a kid faces a supernatural threat inside a specific institutional setting.

comp_set.title: It Follows
comp_set.why_it_comps: The curse logic, adolescent dread, and slow-burn inevitability are close cousins to this script’s pressure-cooker horror.

comp_set.title: The Lodge
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the isolated, psychologically unstable atmosphere and the way the environment itself becomes an engine of dread.

comp_set.title: The Night House
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on grief-adjacent unease, negative-space horror, and a protagonist trying to decode a haunting that feels personal and metaphysical.

audience_target.primary_audience: Horror fans who like atmospheric, mystery-driven genre films with a teen/young-adult emotional core.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 16-34, with a meaningful female audience and strong genre-native male turnout; best fit for viewers who respond to elevated, concept-forward horror.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary boarding-school interiors, a small cast, and minor visual effects keep this in indie-feature territory, with night work and atmospheric design doing most of the heavy lifting.

types_of_buyers: indie financiers looking for a low-VFX hook title
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of atmospheric, concept-driven horror that sells on premise and mood rather than spectacle. The boarding-school setting and emotional invisibility theme give it a cleaner prestige angle than a standard slasher or possession title.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The Room 111 mythology is strong enough for one film, but there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond the central curse.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The curse is a metaphor with teeth.
strengths.what_it_means: The script turns social invisibility into a literal horror mechanism, which gives the movie a clean thematic identity buyers can pitch in one sentence. That kind of metaphor-forward engine is attractive to streamer genre teams and directors who want elevated material without a huge budget burden.
strengths.evidence: James explains that the room feeds on students who have already started disappearing socially, and Ryan’s own voiceover keeps circling the fear of being unseen.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Room 111 reveal is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: The 1:11 clock motif, the locked room, and the eleven-year pattern create a memorable packageable hook that feels like a real title asset. That helps the project stand out in a crowded horror market where buyers want a clean hook they can market fast.
strengths.evidence: The repeated 1:11 imagery, the yearbook pattern, and the final notebook reveal all lock the mythology into a single visual system.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ryan is built for a breakout performance.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead role gives a young actor a full arc from numb observer to terrified participant to morally compromised savior, which is exactly the kind of showcase that can launch a career. Casting teams and directors looking for a contained genre vehicle will see a role with real emotional range.
strengths.evidence: Ryan’s detached voiceover, his escalating investigation, and the final confrontation where he chooses to write his name into the notebook.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The dorm setting is cheap but story-rich.
strengths.what_it_means: A boarding-school corridor, office, and room system give the film a contained footprint without feeling like a single-room gimmick. That makes the script attractive to producers who want atmosphere and production control in the same package.
strengths.evidence: Most of the script lives in the hallway, dorm room, office, classroom, and adjacent school spaces.

strengths.dimension_or_area: James Walker gives the movie a strong antagonist voice.
strengths.what_it_means: The antagonist is not just a monster; he’s a trapped former victim with a philosophy, which gives the movie a more memorable villain than a standard faceless haunting. That kind of role can attract a strong character actor and elevate the trailer moments.
strengths.evidence: James’s Room 111 monologue about names, forgetting, and students who are already halfway gone.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean elevated-horror package: a contained dorm setting, a marketable supernatural rule, and a lead role that can launch a young actor. The script’s strongest commercial asset is that it sells as both a mystery and a metaphor, which gives buyers a premise they can understand fast and a theme that can travel beyond the genre core.

items.area: The mythology arrives in pieces before it fully locks.
items.detail: The opening is effective as atmosphere, but the audience has to wait through several dorm beats before the Room 111 rules, the eleven-year pattern, and the notebook mechanic fully cohere. That makes the first act more dependent on mood than on immediate narrative certainty, which is a real buyer conversation for a feature.

items.area: Ryan carries most of the emotional load.
items.detail: The script is strongest when it is inside Ryan’s head, but that also means the movie leans hard on one performance lane for much of its runtime. If the lead doesn’t land the numbness-to-panic transition, the whole piece loses a lot of its force.

items.area: The supporting cast is functional, not engine-level.
items.detail: Rhea, James, Mrs. Wesman, Mr. Brusco, and Jeff all do useful work, but only James feels like a true scene-dominating presence. That limits relationship density and makes the film less expandable as a character ensemble than the premise initially suggests.

items.area: The ending resets more than it resolves.
items.detail: The final Room 111 loop and Rhea’s disappearance create a strong sting, but the last movement is more ominous than emotionally conclusive. For a feature buyer, that reads as a stylish button, but it also leaves the audience with a slightly more open-ended finish than the central mystery promises.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise — it’s the degree to which the movie depends on Ryan’s internal state and a mythology that takes a minute to fully click. Buyers will like the hook, but they’ll also notice that the supporting engine is lean and the ending plays as a strong chill rather than a full emotional landing.
